newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign market dominated by W African crude.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign market dominated by W African crude.

text.p: U.S. foreign interest leaned towards West African crudes as pent up European demand and a tight arbitrage continued to stave off North Sea supplies.
Several cargoes of Escravos and Cabinda were seen moved into the U.S. Gulf, with offers also for Forcados.
Escravos traded on an fob basis at Dated Brent plus 46 cts, and Cabinda was seen at Dated Brent minus $1.10, with delivery into the U.S. estimated around second-half Oct.
But North Sea cargo interest was unusually thin.
"It's been dry for two-and-half months," an East Coast trader said, referring to cargoes from the North Sea.
A cargo of Brent was reported traded this week at West Texas Intermediate plus 10 cents cif for early Oct.
The same seller attempted to move another 500,000 barrel cargo but faced lukewarm interest, traders said.
A Gulf Coast refiner purchsed one million barrels of Oseberg earlier this week at WTI plus 25 cents cif, also deemed expensive in light of alternative domestic grades.
The tight Brent/WTI spread at $1.10 a barrel was still considered too narrow.
In the U.S. aftermarket, a U.S. trader bought Nov Brent up to $23.70 a barrel, up 27 cents from the IPE settlement.
Intermonth Oct/Nov Brent moved at 37 cents, and Nov/Dec at 53 cents, slightly lower than during the Lodon session.
